precepts.text: Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not. He keeps it tucked in, which goes against Leviticus 5.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
“This Simon now, of whom we spake afore, having been a betrayer of the money, and of his country, slandered Onias”. Simon of the tribe of Benjamin revealed the secret of the money to the Greeks and then slandered Onias the third, telling them Onias was the one who did that to Heliodorus. This Simon was no damn good.

Now look at the ones who stand next to that kind of man: “Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not.”

The type of man who is a partner with it hates his own soul. He hears the cursing and does not tell it. He keeps it tucked in. That goes directly against the law in Leviticus 5, where the one who hears and does not utter it bears the iniquity.

So it is not only the Simon who is guilty. The one who stands by, hears the evil, and keeps quiet is partnered with him, and he is hating his own soul.

precepts.text: If a soul hear the voice of swearing, and is a witness, if he do not utter it, then he shall bear his iniquity. Whatever the judgment is on that man, you get the judgment. This is why in the hood people see murders and say I'm not saying nothing, and later end up dead themselves; they were a witness that chose not to utter it. Story told in class: at camp a brother was told to trim his hair and answered, I guess I'm not traveling then; men heard it, and the officer who heard it first said, I was going to tell you next week. Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me. Be mindful of brothers; you got to be mindful of the things they say or don't say.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
“And if a soul sin, and hear the voice of swearing, and is a witness, whether he hath seen or known of it; if he do not utter it, then he shall bear his iniquity.”

What does that mean? Whatever the judgment is on that man, you get the judgment. This is why in the hood, in the ghetto, people see murders all the time and say, I’m not saying nothing. Then weeks later, a month, a year, that same person ends up dead, and you say, what did she do, they never killed nobody. No: they were a witness, and they chose not to utter it.

Read on and the law also says “if a soul swear, pronouncing with his lips to do evil, or to do good, whatsoever it be that a man shall pronounce with an oath, and it be hid from him; when he knoweth of it, then he shall be guilty in one of these.” And when he is guilty, “he shall confess that he hath sinned in that thing”.

A story from camp: the brothers were planning who to take traveling, and one brother’s hair was unkempt. He was told to trim it, and he answered, well, I guess I’m not traveling then. A couple of men heard it. A young man from Detroit told what was said, and when the officer who heard it first was questioned the next week, he said, I heard it, I was going to tell you next week. Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me.

Be mindful of brothers. They may seem decent on the outside, but you have to be mindful of the things they say, or don’t say.

precepts.text: For I have heard the slander of many: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life. Slander is not a light thing.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
Simon slandered Onias the third. So how serious is slander? “For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life.”

Slander is not a light thing. It is the first step of a counsel against a man’s life. The ones who slander take counsel together, and what they devise is to take away his life.

That is exactly the road Simon walked. He slandered Onias to the Greeks, and it did not stop at words: “when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon’s faction murders were committed”. The slander of many leads to the taking of life.

precepts.text: Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off. There is a lot of slander in the Israelite community; some camps thrive off slander, hatred, name calling, ridicule, and false accusations. God already said I am going to cut slanderers off, so for you to join with these people, you are a fool. And they think God is with them.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
“Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer.”

There is a lot of slander in the Israelite community; Deacon Asaf has been going over it in classes these last two weeks. There are camps that thrive off slander, hatred, name calling, ridicule and false accusations.

God already told you he is going to cut off people who do that. Cut off means he is going to kill them. So for you to join with these people, you are nothing but a fool.

And the high look and the proud heart come from the slander; that is what they do. They think God is with them, and the men and women around them, as stupid as they are, believe God is with them. God is not with them, not according to these scriptures.

precepts.text: Trust ye not in any brother: for every brother will utterly supplant, and every neighbour will walk with slanders. They have taught their tongue to speak lies; there are some very good liars out there.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
“Take ye heed every one of his neighbour, and trust ye not in any brother: for every brother will utterly supplant, and every neighbour will walk with slanders.”

Every neighbour will walk with slanders. “And they will deceive every one his neighbour, and will not speak the truth: they have taught their tongue to speak lies, and weary themselves to commit iniquity.”

There are people who love the slander. They teach their tongue to speak lies, and they are very good at it; there are some very good liars out there. You ever see a woman caught in the midst of adultery? She starts crying: this is not what it looks like. And some men will dismiss what they saw with their own eyes. Some of you are such a simp.

Don’t bring anybody like that around. They cannot roll with us. Let them stay over there with those other camps. That is what Simon was: a brother that supplanted, walked with slanders, and would not speak the truth about Onias.

precepts.text: There be three things that mine heart feareth: the slander of a city, the gathering together of an unruly multitude, and a false accusation: all these are worse than death. Simon did all three: he slandered the city, gathered the Greeks together to get the money from Jerusalem, and falsely accused Onias.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
“There be three things that mine heart feareth; and for the fourth I was sore afraid: the slander of a city, the gathering together of an unruly multitude, and a false accusation: all these are worse than death.”

Simon did all three. The slander of a city: God does not like that thing, and Simon slandered the city. The gathering together of an unruly multitude: Simon had all the Greeks gather together to try to get the money from Jerusalem. And a false accusation: he accused Onias of doing this to Heliodorus. God said all these are worse than death.

Then think about this: don’t tell me what they say about me, tell me why they feel so comfortable telling you. In every school there is that one brother or sister that all the murmurers draw to, and they tell them all the things they don’t like about people. Why do they draw to you? You obviously did not have our back, because they are slandering and they feel so comfortable saying evil to you.

A deacon once pointed out a sister in red shoes with high heels and called her a hoe because of the shoes. The Bishop called Deacon Asaf, Deacon Malachi and the others over and asked them if she was; they said no. And he blew that brother’s spot up in front of them. You cannot come to me with evil. We must train ourselves to hate evil.

precepts.text: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour. These are basic laws, but for some reason in the black community they are so difficult.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
Simon “was he bold to call him a traitor, that had deserved well of the city, and tendered his own nation, and was so zealous of the laws.” He was so bold he called Onias the high priest a traitor, that type of a brother, a man zealous of the law.

The law is plain: “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.” Don’t bear false witness.

These are basic laws, but for some reason in the black community they are so difficult. Just so, so difficult. Simon broke this one outright when he falsely accused Onias before the Greeks, and everything that followed came out of that false witness.

precepts.text: A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow. Because that man will get people hurt and get people killed.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
“A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow.”

Why is he a maul, a sword and a sharp arrow? Because that man will get people hurt, and will get people killed. A false witness is a weapon.

That is what Simon’s false witness against Onias became. He called the high priest a traitor, and before long “by one of Simon’s faction murders were committed”. His lie was a sword in the hands of his faction, and it drew blood among his own people.

precepts.text: Use not to make any manner of lie: for the custom thereof is not good.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
“Use not to make any manner of lie: for the custom thereof is not good.”

Use not to make any manner of lie, not a big one and not a small one. The custom of it is not good: when lying becomes your custom, it becomes what you are.

This follows the false witness of Exodus 20:16 and the maul, sword and sharp arrow of Proverbs 25:18. Simon made a custom of lying: he betrayed the money, slandered Onias, and called a man zealous of the law a traitor. These are basic laws, and our people must keep them.

precepts.text: From whence come wars and fightings among you? Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain. Simon wanted the upper hand over Onias and couldn't get it. Ye have not, because ye ask not; and when ye ask and receive not, it is because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts: a lustful purpose that is not for the benefit of the nation.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
“But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon’s faction murders were committed”. Simon hated Onias the third so much that he had one of his men kill one of Onias’s priests. That is why it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins. James shows where it comes from.

“From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members? Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain”. Simon wanted the upper hand over Onias, and he could not get it. So what did he do?

“ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not.” Because you are not praying to the Lord about it. “Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.” When you pray and still do not receive, it is because you ask for the wrong reasons. You have a lustful purpose behind it, a purpose that is not for the benefit of the nation.

This is a self-examination class for all of us: these are the attributes of Simon.

precepts.text: Whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment; the name calling continues the sin, and whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire. That is when God has to step in.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment: But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment”.

It does not start with the murder. It starts with anger at your brother without a cause. “and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council”. Raca means thou fool, vain fellow, and the council there is man’s council.

“but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.” Just continuing the sin, the name calling and all of that, puts you in danger of hell fire. That is when God has to step in.

These are the attributes of Simon, and the class is a self-examination for all of us. Simon’s anger toward Onias turned into slander and name calling, calling him a traitor, and it ended in murder.

precepts.text: Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer. That is Simon. The domino effect: he coveted power, from there it turned to anger, from there to slander, and from there to murder. Holding on to anger is like drinking poison and expecting the other person to die; the only one affected is you.
precepts.point: But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.
precepts.why:
“Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.”

That is Simon. He hated Onias, his brother, and his faction committed murders. This is the domino effect: it starts off as coveting; Simon coveted power. From there it turned to anger, from there to slander, and from there to murder. It is never just one sin, and not only are you affected, the people you sinned against are affected too.

Holding on to anger is like drinking poison and expecting the other person to die. You are drinking poison waiting for somebody else to drop dead, and they are not dropping dead. The only one being affected is you. This goes for men and women.

Onias was the opposite. He went to the king “not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both publick and private”. He did not even go there to accuse Simon. That is the difference between a brother and a betrayer.

precepts.text: Then certain ungodly persons, who hated their own people, went unto the king. You will always have certain ungodly men and women among us who hate their own people. Videos played in class of black commentators on the Carmelo Anthony verdict: one celebrated the guilty verdict and blamed the family for spending the defense fund; another said he was overjoyed there were no black people on the jury. Whatever happened to a jury of your peers? That is the same thing they did back then: an all-white jury, and a judge that allowed it, with connections to the other family. A video was also played of a woman calling black supremacy the most dangerous ideology and saying every race is tired of black people; the teaching point: where does black supremacy exist? She is not the only one who thinks like that, and there are even those calling themselves repented Israelites who think exactly like that. We had a bunch of them leave in 2018.
precepts.point: For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto. Blessed are the peacemakers, but peace does not always work with some people; some spirits are grimy, and at the end of the day they don't want peace with you.
precepts.why:
Simon hated Onias so much that one of his faction murdered one of Onias’s priests, and he got Apollonius, the governor of Coelosyria and Phenice, to rage and “increase Simon’s malice.” Not only did he turn his own group against the high priest; he went to the other nations against him. That is how far your anger goes when you cannot get your way.

That spirit shows up again in 1 Maccabees: “Then came ungodly persons, who hated their own people, went unto the king, and told him that Jonathan besieged the tower.” You will always have that: certain ungodly men and women among us who hate their own people and run to the king.

See how it relates to us today. On the Carmelo Anthony verdict, one black commentator celebrated the guilty verdict and blamed the family for spending the money raised for his defense on houses. Another said he was overjoyed there were no black people on the jury. Whatever happened to a jury of your peers? It is the same thing they did back then: a whole white jury, and a judge who allowed it, with connections to the other family. Whatever the white man did, not guilty; a black man on trial, three or four minutes, guilty.

Then a black woman called black supremacy the most dangerous ideology in the world and said every race is tired of black people, and “we” want y’all gone. Where does black supremacy exist? Nobody has ever seen it. And she is not the only one who thinks like that. There are brothers and sisters calling themselves repented Israelites who think exactly like that; we had a bunch of them leave in 2018.

Onias went to the king “not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all.” The ungodly who hate their own people go to the king to accuse them. That is the difference between Onias and Simon.

precepts.text: Wherefore laying aside all malice, and all guile, and hypocrisies, and envies, and all evil speakings, as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby. If you apply these two verses, everyone will see a substantial change in your life. But if you are the same grimy brother or sister from last year to the year before that, we know you have not been applying 1 Peter 2:1-2.
precepts.point: For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto. Blessed are the peacemakers, but peace does not always work with some people; some spirits are grimy, and at the end of the day they don't want peace with you.
precepts.why:
Onias went to the king “not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both publick and private.” Simon was full of malice, envy and evil speaking. Peter tells us what to do with all of that.

“Wherefore laying aside all malice”: when you give yourself to the Lord, one of the first things you must do in repenting is lay aside all malice. “And all guile”: guile means deceit; put it away from you. “And hypocrisies”: don’t be a hypocrite. “And envies”: whatever envies, hatreds and jealousies you have, put them from you. “And all evil speakings.”

“As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby.” You cast those sins away and start all over again as newborn babes, desiring the commandments in Christ. That is the only way you can grow in this truth.

If you apply verses 1 and 2, everyone will see a substantial change in your life. But if you are the same grimy brother or sister from last year and the year before that, we know you have not been applying 1 Peter 2:1-2. Our people forget history quickly; we cannot afford to become Simon.

precepts.text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
precepts.point: For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto. Blessed are the peacemakers, but peace does not always work with some people; some spirits are grimy, and at the end of the day they don't want peace with you.
precepts.why:
Onias the high priest went to the king “not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both publick and private.” He did not even go there to accuse Simon. That shows the character of Onias III, a great and upstanding elder man.

Christ says, “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.” That is the attribute of Onias. His own people had turned on him, Simon had one of his priests murdered, and the governor was raging against him, and still he went seeking the good of all, public and private, not revenge.

That is what a child of God does. Simon’s spirit lusts, envies, slanders and kills to get the upper hand. The peacemaker seeks the good of the whole nation.

precepts.text: If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. That is: if it be possible.
precepts.point: For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto. Blessed are the peacemakers, but peace does not always work with some people; some spirits are grimy, and at the end of the day they don't want peace with you.
precepts.why:
Onias sought peace, going to the king seeking the good of all rather than to accuse his countrymen. That is one of his attributes, and Paul gives the rule: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.”

Notice the words: if it be possible. As much as lies in you, you live peaceably. But it is not always possible. Onias “saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto.” Simon was causing insurrections in Jerusalem, and Onias wanted the king to look into it.

Blessed are the peacemakers, and live peaceably if at all possible, but peace doesn’t always work with some people. Some spirits are grimy, and at the end of the day they don’t want peace with you. They want you dead. Onias did everything that lay in him; the rest he took to the king.

precepts.text: Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord.
precepts.point: For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto. Blessed are the peacemakers, but peace does not always work with some people; some spirits are grimy, and at the end of the day they don't want peace with you.
precepts.why:
Onias’s attributes are the attributes of a man of God. He went to the king “not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all.” Hebrews tells us to walk the same way: “Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord.”

Follow peace with all men, and holiness with it. Without them no man shall see the Lord. You cannot see the Lord walking in Simon’s spirit of malice, slander and murder.

Onias followed peace and holiness even when his friend Simon turned on him, and soon after his own blood brother Jason labored underhand to take the priesthood from him. Put yourself in his sandals. He still sought peace, until he saw it was impossible for the state to stay quiet and Simon to leave his folly unless the king looked into it.

precepts.text: Pray that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith. Some men you cannot reason with; there is no sitting down with two witnesses. There are Israelite camps like that: a brother said shalom to one of their men and got cursed out for it. They have no faith; they are teaching now that Moses is in a lake of fire and that John the Baptist was a wicked Israelite. Blasphemous doctrines, filled with hatred, and unreasonable.
precepts.point: For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto. Blessed are the peacemakers, but peace does not always work with some people; some spirits are grimy, and at the end of the day they don't want peace with you.
precepts.why:
Onias saw “that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto.” We read, blessed are the peacemakers, and if it be possible, live peaceably with all men. But peace doesn’t always work with some people.

Paul says: “Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may have free course, and be glorified, even as it is with you: And that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith.” Meditate on that. Some men you cannot reason with. There is no, let’s sit down and talk, let’s get two witnesses. Some spirits are grimy. At the end of the day they don’t want peace with you; they want you dead.

There are Israelite camps like that. Brothers were at an event, and one of these camps was walking by; a brother said shalom to one of their men, and he cursed him out for it. These are unreasonable and wicked men.

They have no faith, and here is how we know: they are teaching now that Moses is in a lake of fire, and that John the Baptist was a wicked Israelite. Blasphemous new doctrines. They are filled with hatred, and they are unreasonable. We pray to be delivered from them, just as Onias could not make peace with Simon and had to take it to the king.

precepts.text: Seek not of the Lord preeminence, neither of the king the seat of honour. The priesthood fell to Onias III; that was his lot. His brother said, I want it; I should have it.
precepts.point: For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God. Sometimes we take the laws of the Most High for granted with the mentality, I can sin and God won't do nothing.
precepts.why:
“Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be high priest.” This is Onias III’s own blood brother. Not only does Onias have to deal with Simon of the tribe of Benjamin; now his brother is trying to take the priesthood from him. When problems come, they come. Put yourself in his sandals: his good friend Simon turned on him, and now his own brother.

Sirach speaks to it: “Seek not of the Lord preeminence, neither of the king the seat of honour.” Why go there? The priesthood fell to Onias III; that was his lot. His brother said, I want it, I should have it, not my brother.

“justify not thyself before the Lord; and boast not of thy wisdom before the king.” Jason went to the king to get what the Lord had not given him, seeking preeminence and the seat of honour, and he bought it.

Sometimes it is not good enough for a brother to be the support brother. Onias was the high priest, and his brother should have supported him. Jason said, I think I can do a better job, and have access to all that money. You have to look at a man’s motives.

precepts.text: If a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully. You want to be an officer, a captain, a deacon; you are not crowned except you strive lawfully. Story told in class: a brother who kept failing the officer of 50 test got a copy of the answers and disseminated it. You might think it is just cheating. No: officers of 50 counsel people. Now a brother who could not pass it is counseling marriages, and he is not qualified for that rank yet. Counsel must be accurate, on point, and scriptural, not from your heart.
precepts.point: For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God. Sometimes we take the laws of the Most High for granted with the mentality, I can sin and God won't do nothing.
precepts.why:
Jason undermined his own brother to become high priest. All of this ties into us today. “And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully.” You want to be an officer, a captain, a deacon, a bishop; you want to be moved up. You are not crowned except you strive lawfully.

Just as Jason undermined his brother, we have had brothers in here do the same thing. A brother said, we keep failing the officer of 50 test; I’ll get a copy with the answers and disseminate it. You might think, oh, it’s just cheating. No. It is worse than that. The officers of 50 counsel people. Now you have a brother who couldn’t pass it, who cheated and became an officer of 50, and he is counseling marriages. Y’all don’t see nothing wrong with that?

He is not qualified for that rank yet. The captains and deacons spend time on the exam, with variations on it, to see each man’s level of understanding, and a lot of it is counseling questions. The counselors mostly come from married men, and counsel must be accurate, on point and scriptural, not from your heart.

That is striving unlawfully, the same as Jason buying the priesthood. And a man who strives that way is not crowned.

precepts.text: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day.
precepts.point: For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God. Sometimes we take the laws of the Most High for granted with the mentality, I can sin and God won't do nothing.
precepts.why:
Paul said a man is not crowned “except he strive lawfully.” What does he mean by crowned? He tells it in the same book: “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.”

The crown is not a rank a man buys or cheats his way into, like Jason bribing the king for the high priesthood. It is a crown of righteousness laid up by the Lord, the righteous judge, and given at that day to those who strove lawfully and love his appearing.

So the brother who wants to be moved up, to be an officer, a captain, a deacon, must remember whose crown he is striving for. Jason got the rule in his hand for a time, but the writer of Maccabees still calls him “that ungodly wretch, and no high priest.”

precepts.text: In the midst of them there was a young man of a high stature, taller than all the rest, and upon every one of their heads he set crowns. Christ is a young man; he was crucified at 33, so art department, don't make him look old. And taller than all the rest means by feet, not inches. These be they that have put off the mortal clothing, and put on the immortal, and have confessed the name of God; it is the Son of God, whom they have confessed in the world, that crowneth them and giveth them palms.
precepts.point: For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God. Sometimes we take the laws of the Most High for granted with the mentality, I can sin and God won't do nothing.
precepts.why:
Who is it that gives out the crowns? Ezra saw it: “And in the midst of them there was a young man of a high stature, taller than all the rest, and upon every one of their heads he set crowns, and was more exalted; which I marvelled at greatly.”

Christ is a young man. He was crucified at 33, so art department, don’t make him look old. And taller than all the rest doesn’t mean by a couple of inches; it means by feet. You are going to know, that’s the Son of God right there, no question.

“So I asked the angel, and said, Sir, what are these? He answered and said unto me, These be they that have put off the mortal clothing, and put on the immortal, and have confessed the name of God: now are they crowned, and receive palms.” This is what we all want.

“Then said I unto the angel, What young person is it that crowneth them, and giveth them palms in their hands? So he answered and said unto me, It is the Son of God, whom they have confessed in the world. Then began I greatly to commend them that stood so stiffly for the name of the Lord.”

The crown comes from Christ, to those who confessed him and stood stiffly for the name of the Lord. It cannot be bought from a king the way Jason bought the priesthood, or cheated for the way a brother cheated the officer of 50 test.

precepts.text: For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins: they afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right.
precepts.point: For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God. Sometimes we take the laws of the Most High for granted with the mentality, I can sin and God won't do nothing.
precepts.why:
Jason promised the king “by intercession three hundred and threescore talents of silver, and of another revenue eighty talents.” What is that called? Bribery. He tried to bribe his way to become high priest. He paid money for an office that goes through bloodline.

Amos shows what the Lord thinks of it: “For I know your manifold transgressions and your mighty sins: they afflict the just, they take a bribe, and they turn aside the poor in the gate from their right.”

That is what they were doing back then. They take a bribe, they afflict the just, and the poor are turned aside from their right. Jason paid the bribe, the king took it, and Onias, the just high priest, was pushed out. The Lord knows those manifold transgressions and mighty sins.

precepts.text: All bribery and injustice shall be blotted out: but true dealing shall endure for ever. The Most High deals with bribes.
precepts.point: For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God. Sometimes we take the laws of the Most High for granted with the mentality, I can sin and God won't do nothing.
precepts.why:
Jason bought the high priesthood with bribes, and three years later he got a taste of it himself: Menelaus, Simon’s brother, offered the king three hundred talents of silver more than Jason and “got the priesthood to himself.” Jason, who had undermined his own brother, was undermined by another and had to flee into the country of the Ammonites.

Sirach says: “All bribery and injustice shall be blotted out: but true dealing shall endure for ever.” The Most High deals with bribes. Here comes Jason, the brother of Onias the high priest, trying to bribe his way in, and it is blotted out.

Sometimes it is not good enough for a brother to be the support brother. Onias was high priest and his brother should have supported him, but Jason said, I can do a better job, plus have access to all that money. Look at a man’s motives. Bribery does not last; true dealing endures for ever.

precepts.text: Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led. That goes back to what we just read: this is when we became Greek citizens and worshiped idols. Everything Paul writes is referenced in the histories; Paul didn't just make stuff up. Where can we find it? In the book of Maccabees, which Esau conveniently took out, so our people in Christianity are lost and confused.
precepts.point: For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God. Sometimes we take the laws of the Most High for granted with the mentality, I can sin and God won't do nothing.
precepts.why:
Jason “forthwith brought his own nation to Greekish fashion.” He built a place of exercise, brought the chief young men under his subjection and made them wear a hat, the hat of Hermes. “Now such was the height of Greek fashions, and increase of heathenish manners.” This is when we became Greek citizens, and we worshiped idols.

That is why Paul says: “Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant. Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led.” That goes back to what we just read. We were led by Jason into heathenish manners and carried away unto dumb idols.

Everything Paul writes is referenced in the histories. Paul didn’t just make stuff up; it was based on something. Where in the Bible do we find it? In the book of Maccabees, which Esau conveniently took out, so our people in Christianity are lost and confused.

All you men that teach on the street must know this history. Verses 10 to 16 sum up what Paul constantly referenced when he said there is neither Jew nor Greek: we followed the Greeks’ customs so earnestly and desired to be like them in all things.

precepts.text: Then shall they be in pitiful case, which now have abused my ways, and they that have cast them away despitefully shall dwell in torments. For such as in their life have received benefits, and have not known me, and they that have loathed my law, while they had yet liberty, and when as yet place of repentance was open unto them, understood not, but despised it; the same must know it after death by pain. Discussed in class: a commentator who said he is not oppressed because he makes ten million dollars a year; that is a benefit received while not knowing God. precepts.why:
“For it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God.” Sometimes we take God’s laws for granted with the mentality, I can sin and God won’t do nothing. Ezra shows otherwise: “Then shall they be in pitiful case, which now have abused my ways: and they that have cast them away despitefully shall dwell in torments.”

“For such as in their life have received benefits, and have not known me.” Look at Jason Whitlock. In the interview he said he is not oppressed because he makes ten million dollars a year. That is a benefit. A lot of our people become doctors and make big money and say, if I can do it, you can do it, and they do not know God. Whitlock once posted Revelation 3:9 on his Instagram with no commentary, all Amalek attacked him, and he quickly deleted it. These people need a wake-up call.

“And they that have loathed my law, while they had yet liberty, and, when as yet place of repentance was open unto them, understood not, but despised it.” They had liberty, because the brothers are out there teaching and the videos are in their feed. They see it, and they hate it.

“The same must know it after death by pain.” So who says that when you die you don’t get punished? You are going to know pain after you die, when Christ returns. Nobody escapes. That is why it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of God, as Jason did.

precepts.text: For the work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways. However you deal in this earth with your brother and your neighbor, it is going to come back on you.
precepts.point: Not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man, because Onias had a good report even among the other nations. The king was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger, he took away Andronicus his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city unto that very place where he had committed impiety against Onias, and there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.
precepts.why:
“Then Jason, who had undermined his own brother, being undermined by another, was compelled to flee into the country of the Ammonites.” Jason undermined his own brother Onias to become high priest, and then he got undermined by Menelaus, the brother of Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin. Now the high priest is of the tribe of Benjamin. You can't make this stuff up.

That is why Job 34:11 is here: “For the work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways.” Whatever you do is going to come back on you. However you deal in this earth with your brother, with your neighbor, it is going to come back on you.

Jason sent Menelaus to bear the money to the king, and Menelaus flattered the king and “got the priesthood to himself, offering more than Jason by three hundred talents of silver.” Jason found the same thing he had done to his brother, and had to run. And later in the history the same thing comes back again on Jason and on Menelaus both: all that evil comes back on them.

precepts.text: He that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done: and there is no respect of persons. The world calls it karma; the Bible says you shall receive for the wrong you have done.
precepts.point: Not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man, because Onias had a good report even among the other nations. The king was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger, he took away Andronicus his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city unto that very place where he had committed impiety against Onias, and there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.
precepts.why:
Here is an easier verse to say what Job 34:11 says: “But he that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done: and there is no respect of persons.” You see how God gets down. In the world they call that karma. The Bible says if you do wrong, you shall receive for the wrong you have done.

There is no respect of persons. Jason was the high priest and it did not protect him: he undermined his own brother and was undermined by another. Andronicus was a man in authority, the king's deputy, and it did not protect him either. He came to Onias in deceit, gave him his right hand with oaths, drew him out of the sanctuary and killed him, and the king took away his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city “unto that very place, where he had committed impiety against Onias, there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.” He received for the wrong he had done, in the very place he did it.

precepts.text: Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. If you decide to undermine the brother next to you or do deceitful stuff to your sister, it is going to come back to you. It might not be this year; it might be next year, but it is going to come.
precepts.point: Not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man, because Onias had a good report even among the other nations. The king was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger, he took away Andronicus his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city unto that very place where he had committed impiety against Onias, and there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.
precepts.why:
“Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.” Don't be deceived, brothers and sisters. God is not mocked. Whatsoever you do in this earth, you are going to reap from what you have done.

So if you decide, I'm going to undermine my brother next to me, I'm going to do some deceitful stuff to my sister, it is going to come back to you. It might not be this year; it might be next year, but it is going to come.

That is the history of 2 Maccabees 4. Jason sowed undermining against his own brother and reaped being undermined by another, “compelled to flee into the country of the Ammonites.” Menelaus got the principality by flattery and money and went on to steal vessels of gold out of the temple, and Andronicus sowed deceit and murder against Onias and reaped death in that very place. Brothers turning on brothers for position all reap what they sow.

precepts.text: Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to thy neighbour; remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance. Sometimes brothers and sisters do something simple; wink at it. It does not always have to be a counsel for small matters. Abstain from strife, and thou shalt diminish thy sins. If thou blow the spark, it shall burn: if thou spit upon it, it shall be quenched: and both these come out of thy mouth. A backbiting tongue hath disquieted many, and driven them from nation to nation: we just read that Onias had to flee from Jerusalem to Syria. It hath pulled down strong cities, and overthrown the houses of great men.
precepts.point: Not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man, because Onias had a good report even among the other nations. The king was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger, he took away Andronicus his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city unto that very place where he had committed impiety against Onias, and there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.
precepts.why:
When Onias found out Menelaus was stealing vessels of gold out of the temple, he reproved him and had to run for his life, fleeing from Jerusalem up to the sanctuary at Daphne by Antiochia in Syria. Sirach shows what drives a man like that from his place.

“Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to thy neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.” Sometimes brothers and sisters may do something simple. Wink at it. It doesn't always have to be a counsel for small matters. “Abstain from strife, and thou shalt diminish thy sins: for a furious man will kindle strife”, and “A sinful man disquieteth friends, and maketh debate among them that be at peace.”

“An hasty contention kindleth a fire: and an hasty fighting sheddeth blood. If thou blow the spark, it shall burn: if thou spit upon it, it shall be quenched: and both these come out of thy mouth.” Your mouth has the power: you can blow on that spark and it will burn, or you can spit on it, let it go, and quench it.

“Curse the whisperer and doubletongued: for such have destroyed many that were at peace. A backbiting tongue hath disquieted many, and driven them from nation to nation”. We just read that Onias had to flee from Jerusalem up to Syria. “strong cities hath it pulled down, and overthrown the houses of great men.” A backbiting tongue overthrew the house of a great man, Onias, the real high priest.

precepts.text: Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without. Onias had a good report among the Jews and the other nations, and he was not trying to join with the other nations. Without means outside the truth: you must have a good report outside this truth.
precepts.point: Not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man, because Onias had a good report even among the other nations. The king was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger, he took away Andronicus his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city unto that very place where he had committed impiety against Onias, and there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.
precepts.why:
When Onias was murdered, “not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man”, and even Antiochus “was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead.” The white man was crying for Onias, because other nations respected Onias III.

That is his character. He had a good report among the Jews and among the other nations, and he was not trying to join with the other nations; he said, I'm not joining with you. But he still had a good report among them. “Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.”

“Without” means without the truth. You must have a good report outside this truth. If we are at camp one day and somebody tries to do a drive-by on us because of something you did or said, what the hell is going on here? You have to have a good report within and without, like Onias.

precepts.text: That ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing. You can't be outside this school robbing, stealing, lying, using drugs, whatever little secret things you have going on. Why lack of nothing? Because people are going to look out for you in the world: this is a good brother, a good sister right here.

The king was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger, he took away Andronicus his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city unto that very place where he had committed impiety against Onias, and there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.
precepts.why:
Somebody might say a good report with them that are without is only for somebody that desires the office of a bishop. No: “That ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing.”

You have to walk honestly toward them that are without the truth. You can't be outside the school, outside this truth, robbing, stealing, lying, using drugs, whatever little secret things you have going on.

Why “lack of nothing”? Because people are going to look out for you out there in the world. They are going to say, now this is a good dude, this is a good sister right here. That is what Onias had: a sober and modest behaviour that even the other nations honored, so that when he was slain without cause, they complained with the Jews.

precepts.text: Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time. Be aware of the time you are in.
precepts.point: Not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man, because Onias had a good report even among the other nations. The king was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger, he took away Andronicus his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city unto that very place where he had committed impiety against Onias, and there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.
precepts.why:
“Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time.” Walk in wisdom toward them that are without the truth, that don't know the truth.

“Redeeming the time” means be aware of the time you are in.

It goes with the good report of Onias. He had a good report among the Jews and among the other nations without joining himself to the other nations, and when he was unjustly murdered, the Jews and “certain of the Greeks that abhorred the fact also” complained because he “was slain without cause.” That is walking in wisdom toward them that are without: keeping yourself apart from their ways, and still carrying yourself so that they know you are righteous.

precepts.text: Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation. Our people living like Gentiles will repent based on your conduct out there in the world.

The king was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger, he took away Andronicus his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city unto that very place where he had committed impiety against Onias, and there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.
precepts.why:
“Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.”

They may speak against us as evildoers, but they shall behold our good works. Why would they glorify God? Because our people who are living like Gentiles will repent based on your conduct out there in the world.

That is the lesson of Onias in 2 Maccabees 4. His conduct was honest before the nations, and even the Greeks and the king wept for him. Menelaus and Andronicus dealt in flattery, theft and deceit, and they brought reproach. Our conversation outside this truth is how our own people living like Gentiles will see it and come to repentance.

precepts.text: When Antiochus Epiphanes took the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be high priest, promising the king three hundred and threescore talents of silver and eighty more, and a hundred and fifty more if he might set him up a place for exercise, a gym, for the training up of youth in the fashions of the heathen, and write them of Jerusalem by the name of Antiochians. A wicked Israelite who took a Greek name, bribed the white man to remove his righteous brother, and Greekified the youth. When a man seeks leadership, he usually is not meant to lead.
precepts.point: If ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise. Romans 9:3-5: Paul's kinsmen according to the flesh, Israelites, to whom pertaineth the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service of God, and the promises, whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came. The heirs are Israelites.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walking Through Galatians

precepts.why:
How did Israelites become Greeks? “But after the death of Seleucus, when Antiochus, called Epiphanes, took the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be high priest”. Jason was a wicked Israelite who changed his name to Jason, a Greek name. He sought underhandedly to be high priest against his brother Onias, a righteous man, using money to gain authority and leadership. When a man seeks leadership, he usually is not meant to be a leader at all.

“Promising unto the king by intercession three hundred and threescore talents of silver, and of another revenue eighty talents”. He bribed the king of the Greeks, the white man, to force his brother out of position and put him in. “Beside this, he promised to assign an hundred and fifty more, if he might have licence to set him up a place for exercise”, a gym, “and for the training up of youth in the fashions of the heathen”: training the Israelite youth in the culture of the Greeks.

“and to write them of Jerusalem by the name of Antiochians.” He registered the Israelites of Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch, the Antioch in Turkey that Paul writes about. Becoming Antiochians was a betrayal of the ancestral laws and a shift to the Greek way of life, and that cultural tension triggered the Maccabean revolt. Antiochian and Greek are the same.

So when Paul says “There is neither Jew nor Greek”, he is writing to the descendants of those same people. Whether called Jew or Greek, “if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.” The heirs are Israelites, to whom pertain the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law and the promises.

precepts.text: Those with Simon were persuaded for money to let the enemy go, and Judas slew the traitors.
precepts.point: Menelaus outbid him for the priesthood, and Jason turned and slew his own people. The seekers of the white man's glory do the same today.

note.label: All Skinfolk Ain't Kinfolk: Children of Darkness

precepts.why:
Simon was “a betrayer of the money, and of his country”, and he slandered Onias, the righteous high priest, trying to get him taken out to replace him. After him came Jason, Onias’s own brother, another house negro, who labored underhand to be high priest; and then Menelaus, Simon’s brother, who outbid Jason for the priesthood. Simon, Jason, Menelaus: all traitors of their own people.

The betrayal for money did not stop with them. When Maccabeus and his men “ran with violence upon the strong holds of the Idumeans”, they killed no fewer than twenty thousand, and about nine thousand fled into two very strong castles. Maccabeus left Simon, Joseph and Zaccheus to besiege them and went where he was needed more.

“Now they that were with Simon, being led with covetousness, were persuaded for money through certain of those that were in the castle, and took seventy thousand drachms, and let some of them escape.” The enemy in the castle bribed them: let us escape and we will pay you. They took the money and let them go.

When Maccabeus heard it, he “accused those men, that they had sold their brethren for money, and set their enemies free to fight against them.” They sold out their own brothers. “So he slew those that were found traitors, and immediately took the two castles.” That is what was done to traitors back then: they got death.

So from Simon slandering Onias to the men selling their brethren for seventy thousand drachms, it is the same spirit. All skinfolk ain’t kinfolk. There were always those among us making a covenant with hell and death for money and the white man’s favor, even until now.

precepts.text: The chief priests and the Pharisees feared that Rome would take away their place and nation, because Rome was who gave them their seats of authority. It was the same from the time of the Maccabees: the white man decides who sits in the seats of power, and the black minister still has to go to his schools to get his.
precepts.point: The moment he had the rule he brought his own nation to the Greekish fashion, and that is exactly what black Christianity does today: it wants our people under white supremacy and in the fashion of the heathen.

precepts.text: The scribes and Pharisees charged the disciples with transgressing the tradition of the elders, and Christ asked them why they transgress the commandment of God by their tradition. Traditions are what Christians teach: white Jesus, Sunday worship, Christmas, New Year's Eve, Mother's Day. If you want to know who the Pharisees are today, it is them.
precepts.point: The moment he had the rule he brought his own nation to the Greekish fashion, and that is exactly what black Christianity does today: it wants our people under white supremacy and in the fashion of the heathen.

precepts.text: The Greeks used the same strategy, taking our chief young men and teaching them heathenish Grecian ways, and they still do this today through sports academies.
precepts.point: When our people do well financially, get a good education, and buy into the pick-yourself-up-by-the-bootstraps idea that everyone has the same opportunity, the smart ones are removed from the ghetto so they will not be there to cause the uprising.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

precepts.why:
The Greeks used the same strategy as Babylon. Jason, “that ungodly wretch, and no high priest”, built “a place of exercise under the tower itself, and brought the chief young men under his subjection, and made them wear a hat.” The chief young men, the mighty of the land, brought under Greek subjection.

Such was “the height of Greek fashions, and increase of heathenish manners” that the priests “had no courage to serve any more at the altar”. They despised the temple, neglected the sacrifices and hastened to the place of exercise “after the game of Discus called them forth”, “Not setting by the honours of their fathers, but liking the glory of the Grecians best of all.”

Take the best and brightest, teach them heathenish Grecian ways, and they turn from their fathers to the glory of the oppressor. They still do this today through sports academies. It is the mighty of the land taken, so the kingdom stays base.

precepts.text: Jason bought the high priesthood by intercession and set up a gymnasium to train the youth in the fashions of the heathen, Israel getting in league with the heathen.
precepts.point: With the arms of a flood they are overflown and broken from before him, yea also the prince of the covenant, and after the league made with him he works deceitfully.

note.label: Daniel 11: The Kings of the North and the South

precepts.why:
“But after the death of Seleucus, when Antiochus, called Epiphanes, took the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be high priest”. points: This Simon, having been a bewrayer of the money and of his country, slandered Onias, as if he had terrified Heliodorus and been the worker of these evils. But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.

Onias, seeing the danger of this contention, and that Apollonius as governor of Coelosyria and Phenice did rage and increase Simon's malice, went to the king: not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both public and private. For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto. Blessed are the peacemakers, but peace does not always work with some people; some spirits are grimy, and at the end of the day they don't want peace with you.

After the death of Seleucus, when Antiochus called Epiphanes took the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be high priest. This is his own blood brother. Put yourself in his sandals: his good friend Simon turned on him, and now his brother.

Jason promised the king by intercession three hundred and threescore talents of silver, and of another revenue fourscore talents. That is called bribery. And the priesthood goes through bloodline. Beside this, he promised to assign an hundred and fifty more, if he might have licence to set him up a place for exercise, and for the training up of youth in the fashions of the heathen. By reason whereof sore calamity came upon them: for they had them to be their enemies and avengers, whose custom they followed so earnestly, and unto whom they desired to be like in all things. Three years afterward Jason sent Menelaus, the aforesaid Simon's brother, to bear the money unto the king. Remember Simon of the tribe of Benjamin: his brother is Menelaus. But he, being brought to the presence of the king, magnified him for the glorious appearance of his power, and got the priesthood to himself, offering more than Jason by three hundred talents of silver. He came bringing nothing worthy the high priesthood, but having the fury of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast.

Then Jason, who had undermined his own brother, being undermined by another, was compelled to flee into the country of the Ammonites. Now the high priest is of the tribe of Benjamin. You cannot make this stuff up.

Menelaus, supposing that he had gotten a convenient time, stole certain vessels of gold out of the temple, gave some of them to Andronicus, and sold some into Tyrus and the cities round about. When Onias knew of a surety, he reproved him, and withdrew himself into a sanctuary at Daphne, by Antiochia; the map was shown in class of where Onias had to flee.

Jason brought in Greek fashions and a place of exercise, and the priests left the altar to watch the games, liking the glory of the Grecians best of all.
